doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Sixties: Verve end, California, Half Note, Duets
title: The 'Motion' sessions with Elvin Jones and Nick Stabulas
summary: They dispute the discography about the Stabulas and Elvin Jones sessions and Creed Taylor ending his contract.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: I want to talk to you about that in a little bit. The next major record is Motion in sixty-one. You did two days of recording with Sonny Dallas and Nick Stabulas and then you decided for whatever reason to shelve all of that and hire Elvin and do another date with Elvin which became the record.
Wait a minute. I don’t remember that happening. The date was with Elvin. Nick Stabulas was after the fact.
Not according to the dates. The dates they give, you and Sonny did two days with Nick: August seventeenth and August twenty-first.
Which year?

Sixty-one, and then the date with Elvin was a week later, August twenty- ninth and all the stuff that went on the record was the stuff with Elvin and the stuff with Nick stayed in the can until the late nineties when they put out a multi-CD set with everything.
I don’t remember it that way.
What do you remember?

I remember that there was a date with Elvin and Sonny. I had asked Max [Roach] to do it and he’s said he couldn’t do it and he suggested Elvin. That’s the way it started. Then I wanted to do another day with Elvin and he was traveling so I asked Nick.
That’s very curious because there’s much more stuff with Nick. There’s about, oh god, fifteen to twenty titles with Nick from two days of recording.
I think those dates are wrong.
Okay. That’s certainly possible. Discographies are far from engraved in stone.

With my faulty memory you kind of verified that “Birth of the Cool” thing. I was told so many times that there was a gig here and a gig there in addition which I couldn’t remember. So that was verified and this must be verifiable.
It’s very curious to me because the stuff with Nick to my ears sounds fine.
I like that, sure.

The stuff with Elvin is great too, it’s just two very different kinds of drummers. It’s understandable why the stuff with Elvin perhaps came out first, the original Motion album, because Elvin was hot at the time and he played great for you and you sounded great on the record.
You noticed he used a middle name on that?
Elvin “Ray” Jones, yes. Why was that?
I think it had to do with color maybe.
That was his choice then?
I don’t know whose choice it was but why all of the sudden a “Ray” Jones somehow not wanting to identify with that situation.
What do you remember about those dates? About the way you felt playing? How did you feel about playing with Elvin?
Great. I was looking forward to doing some more as I’m suggesting. The man in charge then . . .
Creed Taylor?
Creed Taylor, let me go, canceled my contract after that record, I believe.
He was eliminating a lot of people’s contracts at the time.
I was one of them. I don’t know when the Nick Stabulas one was but I think it was connected soon enough not like years later when we found out Elvin wasn’t available.

Actually, in the liner notes to the three CD release that came out in the late nineties of Motion, Sonny Dallas was quoting on saying that Nick’s playing wasn’t up to his usual standard which was why Elvin was called. That’s what Sonny said for what it’s worth.
There’s no way to verify that except through some kind of examining of the books.

Yeah, by looking at the original session logs. Those are the dates they give: August seventeenth and twenty-first with Nick and August twenty-ninth with Elvin. Go figure. So after that you’re out of a recording contract and basically . . .
How long was I with Verve?
Fifty-eight through sixty-one.
Three years again.
Yeah. The Image record was you first one and the Motion record was your last one for Verve.
